speaker: Sholto Douglas
title: Is RL + LLMs enough for AGI? — Sholto Douglas & Trenton Bricken
question: In frontier AI labs, why did models achieve breakthroughs in math and software engineering much earlier than in general computer use and office workflows?
guest: The only difference with computer use is that it's slightly harder to pose into clean feedback loops than math and coding. I also think it's underappreciated how far from a perfect machine these labs are. It's not like you have a thousand people optimizing computer use. Everything at these labs is best-effort pulled together under incredible time pressure and constraints, with incredibly difficult prioritization problems. Coding is immensely valuable right now and somewhat more tractable, so it makes sense to devote more effort to coding initially because there's super-exponential value as you get closer to solving a domain, rather than allocating the marginal person toward computer use. Everyone is making these difficult trade-off calls. Also, funnily enough, researchers at the labs love working on the bars of intelligence that they themselves resonate with. That's why math and competitive programming fell first—to everyone at the labs, that's their bar of intelligence. It's like, 'If it can beat me at AIME, then that's smart,' not 'If it can do an Excel model better than me.' So we've reached the point where people respect it, we just haven't invested as much effort in the other areas.

points.note: Accept: concentrating marginal effort on an already tractable, high-value domain near completion yields far higher payoff than spreading talent thin on earlier-stage domains. Do not credit: simply noting coding is popular.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Several reinforcing factors explain the gap, and most come down to how well each domain suits the way models are trained.

Math and code are natively textual, so they match the modality language models handle best. The internet also supplies enormous amounts of high-quality training data: GitHub, Stack Overflow, textbooks, and proofs. Computer use, by contrast, requires visually perceiving screens and performing precise clicks, and almost no one records detailed traces of how they navigate spreadsheets or enterprise software.

Verification matters just as much. Code can be run against tests and proofs can be formally checked, which gives cheap, automatic, unambiguous reward signals for reinforcement learning and for benchmarks. Office tasks have fuzzy success criteria, such as whether a report was "good", and they are expensive to grade at scale.

Office workflows also involve long chains of actions across messy, stateful environments, where small errors compound and mistakes can be irreversible. They depend on tacit organizational context that is rarely written down.

Finally, labs prioritized coding because their researchers are themselves programmers, the commercial demand was immediate, and coding ability accelerates AI research itself.

points.why: The response directly explains why office workflows are harder to turn into verifiable reinforcement learning environments than math and coding.
quotes: Code can be run against tests and proofs can be formally checked, which gives cheap, automatic, unambiguous reward signals for reinforcement learning and for benchmarks.
Office tasks have fuzzy success criteria, such as whether a report was "good", and they are expensive to grade at scale.

The response cites immediate demand and research acceleration without explaining how nearing a solution increases the payoff from allocating additional researchers to coding.
The response notes that researchers are programmers without linking their choice of benchmarks to what they personally regard as prestigious or as evidence of intelligence.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Math and software engineering matched how frontier models are trained across data, verification, and simulation. Both domains are natively text-based and richly documented on the public web in codebases, papers, and problem archives, whereas office workflows unfold as unrecorded clicks and visual states locked inside private enterprise software.

More importantly, math and code offer objective, automated verification: compilers, unit tests, and answer checkers provide unambiguous signals that enabled large-scale reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards without human grading bottlenecks. Office tasks, by contrast, depend on tacit organizational context and subjective judgment that resist clean programmatic scoring. Execution infrastructure also diverges sharply. Labs can run millions of fast, deterministic code sandboxes in parallel, while general computer use requires heavy virtual machines, multimodal GUI perception, stateful third-party interfaces, and long-horizon action loops where minor pixel-level errors compound. Combined with AI researchers’ ability to directly dogfood coding tools, abundant text data, cheap sandboxes, and crisp verifiers made math and software far easier to scale first.

points.why: The response explains why math and code provide verifiable rewards and why office tasks are harder to score programmatically.

noweb.answer:
Frontier AI models progressed faster in math and software engineering primarily because those domains combine abundant text-native data, cheap sandboxed execution, and objective verification. Public codebases, papers, and forums provided vast pretraining corpora capturing not just final outputs, but explicit reasoning chains, version diffs, and debugging history. Crucially, compilers, unit tests, and exact mathematical answers supply fast, deterministic reward signals. Labs could run millions of lightweight, stateless rollouts in parallel, enabling large-scale reinforcement learning and synthetic data generation without human bottlenecks.

General computer use and office workflows lacked these structural advantages. Public data rarely records the tacit, multi-step action traces of workers navigating spreadsheets, browsers, and enterprise software. Acting through graphical interfaces also requires precise visual grounding across brittle, shifting layouts rather than clean text manipulation. Finally, realistic office environments are slow, stateful, and costly to simulate—requiring heavy virtual machines, authentication, and safeguards against real-world side effects—while success on tasks like building a persuasive slide deck or triaging email is subjective, context-dependent, and difficult to grade automatically.

points.why: The response explains why math and coding provide cleaner reward signals than office tasks.
quotes: compilers, unit tests, and exact mathematical answers supply fast, deterministic reward signals
subjective, context-dependent, and difficult to grade automatically

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because math and coding are easy to check, and office work is not. Reinforcement learning, which drove the recent reasoning gains, works best when a program can grade each attempt automatically and cheaply. Unit tests, compilers, proof checkers and known final answers give clean right-or-wrong signals at huge scale, so labs could run millions of practice attempts. Both fields were also already text-heavy, with large stores of public data like GitHub, arXiv and competition problems, which fits how language models work.

Computer use is harder on almost every front. Models have to read screens, find small interface elements and click precisely. Tasks take many steps, so small errors pile up. There is little recorded data of people actually operating software. Training environments are slow and costly to simulate, and they break easily across endless apps and websites. In office work, "success" is often unclear or a matter of taste, so it's hard to grade. Mistakes in real accounts, like sending emails or moving money, carry safety risks that limit open-ended experimentation.

Labs also had a strong reason to prioritize coding, since better coding models speed up their own research.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Math and software engineering broke through first primarily because they are text-native domains with fast, objective verification. A math solution can be checked against a known answer or formal proof checker, and code can be compiled and tested in milliseconds. That allowed frontier labs to scale reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, letting models practice millions of rollouts cheaply in isolated sandboxes with clear pass-or-fail signals. Both fields also benefited from massive public corpora of code, problems, and solutions.

General computer use and office workflows invert nearly every one of those advantages. They unfold across noisy, constantly changing graphical interfaces, span long horizons across multiple apps, and involve real-world side effects that make fast simulation much harder. Crucially, success is rarely binary: judging whether a slide deck, email, or financial report is good depends on tacit context, company norms, and subjective human taste. Without cheap automated verifiers or abundant logged trajectories of expert computer use, scaling post-training has been far slower.

points.why: The response attributes slower progress in computer use to the difficulty of automating feedback that math and coding can verify cheaply.
quotes: Without cheap automated verifiers or abundant logged trajectories of expert computer use, scaling post-training has been far slower.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Math and coding gave frontier labs abundant training data and cheap ways to check whether a model succeeded. A math problem often has a known answer, and a code change can be compiled and tested. In both domains, labs could run many attempts in parallel, use the results to train models, and measure progress on repeatable benchmarks.

General computer use and office work are harder to practice and grade at scale. A task like reconciling a spreadsheet and updating a report can span several apps, depend on private records and unwritten team conventions, and have several acceptable outcomes. Even when the goal is clear, the model has to navigate changing interfaces, manage permissions, and keep track of what it has already done. A small mistake early in the workflow can invalidate the result. That makes realistic training environments costlier to build and reliable feedback harder to obtain.

points.why: The candidate explains why math and coding provide easy-to-verify outcomes while office workflows make reliable training feedback harder to obtain.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
One major reason is that labs could give models fast, reliable feedback in math and coding. A proposed math answer can often be checked automatically, and a code change can be run against tests. That lets a lab train on millions of attempts and measure whether a new model solves more problems. The advantage was greatest on well-specified tasks. Real software projects with unclear requirements are harder for the same reason office work is hard.

General computer use adds two difficulties. First, the model has to act reliably through changing interfaces, where one missed dialog can derail a long sequence. Second, success is harder to judge. A spreadsheet can open and its formulas can run even if it answers the wrong business question. Evaluating that result may require company context and human judgment. Those differences made it harder to build training environments at scale, reward good attempts, and tell whether improvements would carry over to everyday work.
